extracted.intended_audience: academics and scholars in epistemology, media studies, and communication; journalists, media literacy practitioners, and policy-makers interested in conceptualizing and responding to fake news
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and evaluating a working, philosophically informed definition of 'fake news' that distinguishes it from related forms of public disinformation and helps explain its recent proliferation, especially on social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gelfert's stipulative definition (FN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is best defined as the deliberate presentation of (typically) false or misleading claims as news, where the claims are misleading by design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the author's proposed working definition. 'By design' is explicated as systemic features of the process of news production and dissemination that manipulate cognitive processes. The definition is intended to (i) reserve the label for deliberate presentations (distinguishing from honest mistakes), (ii) require presentation in a news-like format, and (iii) emphasize systemic/channel features (particularly relevant for social media) rather than merely content falsity. The definition is to be tested against distinguishing fake news from rumor, hoax, satire, false advertising, and sloppy journalism, and evaluated for its ability to explain the recent proliferation of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading 'by design' / systemic dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The misleading nature of fake news is due to systemic features inherent in the design of the sources and channels through which it propagates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert stresses that beyond individual intent, systemic design (especially of online social media platforms and distribution networks) fosters propagation and targeting, enabling fake news to exploit audience cognitive biases. This includes processes of production and dissemination engineered to produce and amplify misleading beliefs (e.g., through targeted distribution, viral-sharing mechanics, removing traditional editorial markers). This systemic element is offered as central to the novelty and urgency of contemporary fake news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberateness / intention to mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Many definitions require that fake news be intentionally or knowingly false or misleading: 'intentionally or knowingly false statements of fact' (Klein & Wueller), 'intentionally false' (Facebook), 'created with an intention to deceive' (Fake News Challenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper records this frequent criterion but nuances it: individual intentionality is important for legal responsibility and some definitions, yet Gelfert allows that systemic design can render content misleading without requiring every individual actor's explicit malicious intent. Thus intentionality may be sufficient in some accounts but not strictly necessary under the proposed (FN) when systemic design produces misleading outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation as news / mimicry of journalistic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news presents or 'purports to describe events in the real world' and mimics the conventions, format, and content of legitimate journalism (Levy; Rini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion distinguishes fake news from other misleading content (e.g., advertising) by focusing on form: layout, masthead, headline style, reportage conventions. Mimicry of legitimate media helps explain why fake news can be mistaken for real reporting and thus why it can be impactful; it is central to definitions that emphasize resemblance to legitimate media organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and type of falsity (completely fabricated vs. mixtures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some characterizations define fake news as 'completely fabricated' or 'news stories that have no factual basis' (Plothow; Allcott & Gentzkow; Fake News Challenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert critiques definitions that require total fabrication: many fake-news items mix true and false elements or rely on selective presentation/partial truths. Thus defining fake news solely by total falsity is overly restrictive; deliberate misleading can occur through omission, false context, or selective emphasis, not only through wholly invented facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-centric criterion: online / social media circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some accounts treat online publication or wide circulation online as constitutive of fake news (Klein & Wueller; Bakir & McStay; various commentators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the internet and social media are repeatedly identified as key facilitators of contemporary fake news, Gelfert argues medium should not be built into the core definition because fake news can spread across media. Instead, online social media should be seen as an explanans for proliferation (they enable targeting, rapid sharing, and removal of traditional credibility cues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of mis- and disinformation types (Wardle's seven types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news can be usefully classified into types (from most to least harmful): fabricated content (100% false), false context, false connection (misleading headlines), and satire/parody, among others (Claire Wardle's typology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wardle's typology is presented as a pragmatic tool for distinguishing degrees of harm and kinds of distortion. Gelfert references it as helpful background—suggesting fake news is a cluster concept—and to show that not all items labelled 'fake news' are alike. This supports nuanced responses and media-literacy interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctive definition: wholly false OR deliberately misleading elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A disjunctive formulation defines fake news as either wholly false content or content that incorporates deliberately misleading elements in its content or context (Bakir & McStay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures both outright fabrication and cases where partial truth is deployed to mislead. Gelfert notes this is closer to practice but warns it can still overstate degree of fabrication and may blur boundaries with other forms of misinformation unless supplemented by format and systemic criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rini's four-part criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A fake news story: (1) purports to describe events in the real world, typically by mimicking traditional reportage; (2) is known by its creators to be significantly false; and (3) is transmitted with the two goals of being widely re-transmitted and of deceiving at least some of its audience (Rini).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert endorses elements of this account (especially its explanatory power regarding why fake news thrives online) and highlights that Rini's inclusion of creators' knowledge and the twin goals (spread and deception) provide specificity useful for distinguishing cases. He also notes the need to incorporate systemic 'by design' features so as not to rely solely on individual creators' knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levy's format-and-content resemblance criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news is 'the presentation of false claims that purport to be about the world in a format and with a content that resembles the format and content of legitimate media organisations' (Levy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes resemblance to legitimate media and the presentation of claims 'about the world'. Gelfert views this as helpful but incomplete without the systemic/design element that explains modern propagation and manipulation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing fake news from related phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions should differentiate fake news from gossip, rumor, hoaxes, urban legends, satire, false advertising, and sloppy journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert provides criteria for differentiation: scope and audience (gossip vs. universal-interest rumors), intent and expected discovery (hoaxes often intend to be discovered), presentation format (false advertising not presented as news), and systemic/design features (sloppy journalism only counts if misleading 'by design'). These distinctions help allocate appropriate remedies and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of cognitive biases and heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary fake news often exploits cognitive biases (confirmation bias, repetition effects, priming, affective arousal) to induce belief and encourage sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert lists specific mechanisms: confirmation bias (favoring evidence that confirms pre-existing beliefs), repetition/illusory truth, priming with loaded epithets ('Lying Ted', 'Crooked Hillary'), affective arousal increasing partisan polarization, poisoning the well via rhetorical 'fake news' accusations, and phenomena like source confusion and belief perseverance that make debunking ineffective. These mechanisms are part of the 'by design' systemic account and explain why fake news propagates on social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim/goals: wide retransmission and secondary gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Many definitions emphasize that fake news is created with goals: to be widely re-transmitted and often to produce a secondary gain (political influence, financial profit, attention) (Fake News Challenge; Rini; Allcott & Gentzkow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including goals helps distinguish casual misinformation from strategically engineered disinformation. Gelfert notes goals may vary (propaganda, financial motives, trolling) but the systemic mechanics that achieve wide retransmission (targeting, virality) are central to contemporary concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal perspective: intentionality and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: From a legal standpoint, definitions highlighting intentional false statements (Klein & Wueller) are relevant because intentionality can determine liability (e.g., for slander).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert acknowledges that while individual intent matters for legal culpability, conceptual definitions used for social-epistemic analysis should also account for systemic features. Thus legal criteria and conceptual/diagnostic criteria can diverge in emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience competence and media literacy as evaluative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of an audience to detect satire or distinguish fake from real news is relevant: some 'fake news' (e.g., The Daily Show) relies on cues that an attentive audience will spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert discusses how satire and parody presuppose media literacy; when audience competence is low, such formats might be mistaken for deceptive fake news. Media literacy, therefore, is both a mitigator and an evaluative axis when determining harm and appropriate classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate simple falsity with fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors, honest mistakes, or simplifications (e.g., minor inaccuracies) should not automatically be classified as fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gelfert warns against overly broad definitions (e.g., Facebook's 'false news') that would capture ordinary reporting errors or pedagogical simplifications. The distinction rests on deliberate presentation, format, and systemic design rather than mere falsity.
